answer:
Based on my search results, particularly the IMF Fiscal Monitor data and the Eurostat domestic currency data, I found the following percentage changes in general government net debt in domestic currency between January 1, 2019 and December 31, 2021:

**Domestic Currency Values:**
- **Poland (PLN):** 2,123,880 → 2,444,256 = **+15.1%**
- Germany (EUR): 2,701,606 → 2,902,035 = +7.4%
- France (EUR): 3,346,281 → 3,536,068 = +5.7%
- Spain (EUR): 1,667,376 → 1,739,501 = +4.3%
- Italy (EUR): 3,033,575 → 3,158,191 = +4.1%
- Belgium (EUR): 295,654 → 324,576 = +9.8%
- Netherlands (EUR): 490,551 → 517,377 = +5.5%
- Portugal (EUR): 278,244 → 283,106 = +1.7%
- Switzerland (CHF): ~193 → ~208 = +7.8%

Poland had the highest percentage change at approximately 15.1% increase in general government net debt by domestic currency between 2019 and 2021.

Answer: **Poland**

A country’s national debt, also known as government debt or public debt, is defined as all borrowings owed by the government of a country. It usually comprises internal debt – owed to other governmental departments – and external debt, which is held by the public and is owed to government bond owners. National debt can be caused by a struggling economy in general, or by low tax income, which usually leads to money being borrowed from other governments for support, which in turn cannot be paid back right away. At first glance, a high national debt is not always a sign of a struggling economy – but since increasing debt can slow down economic growth significantly, it is imperative for the respective government to seek a steady reduction in the long run.

## Risk factors: interest rates and economic growth
[edit]
Major risk factors that can increase government debt include slowing economic growth and rising interest rates.
Rising interest rates increase public debt charges, raising government expenditures.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Kerim-Dikeni_L%C3%A9onard_20210914-1) From 2011 to 2021, falling interest rates meant that, while public debt rose, public debt charges decreased from $29 billion to $24 billion.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Kerim-Dikeni_L%C3%A9onard_20210914-1) The average interest rate paid on the federal debt was 4.6% in the fiscal year 2007/08,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Kerim-Dikeni_L%C3%A9onard_20210914-1) and in 2020/21 it was 1.4%.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-DFC_2022-42):49 Rates at that time were by far the lowest in the post-war period.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Drummond_20201020-43) By 2024/25, consolidated general government interest expenses reached $102.4 billion ($50.1 billion for the federal government, and $52.5 billion for the provincial, territorial and local governments), due to higher debt refinancing interest rates and higher government gross debt.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Daily20251121-4) Measured as a share of total government revenue, the consolidated general government interest expense in 2024/25 was 9%.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Daily20251121-4)

## Risk factors: interest rates and economic growth
Slow economic growth is a risk factor since it means government tax revenue grows less quickly. Further, slower growth of GDP relative to growth of debt increases the ratio of debt to GDP.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Drummond_20201020-43)

## Debt comparison with other countries
[edit]
The level of government responsible for government programs differs across countries. For this reason, international fiscal comparisons are usually made on a total government, national accounts basis. For Canada, total government includes the federal (central), provincial/territorial, and local governments. Another reason to measure debt on a total government basis is that the federal government may be viewed as responsible for the debt of other levels of government.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-44)Credit rating agency Fitch said it expects the federal government to provide a province with access to debt markets, as it did early in the coronavirus pandemic.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-46) When Newfoundland needed debt repayment assistance in March 2020, it appealed to the federal government.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-47) Any aid delivered to one province would reduce the resources the federal government has available for its own debt repayment responsibilities, and to support debt repayment in other provinces.

## Debt comparison with other countries
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) reports that in 2024 Canada's net and gross debt-to-GDP ratios were 11% and 110%, respectively.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-IMF2026-48) Canada's general government holds sizeable financial assets (approximately 99% measured as a percentage of GDP at market value at end-2024), with around 30% invested in equity shares, of which more than half relate to pension fund investments.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-IMF2026-48):49–50 Financial assets rose sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic (to 81% of GDP in 2021 from 64% in 2019), spurred by support measures such as loans to businesses and tax deferrals (accounts receivable).[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-IMF2022-49):39 Canada's general government gross debt includes substantial accounts payable (around 18% of GDP at end-2024), which many advanced countries do not report.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-IMF2026-48):49–50 In net debt calculations, most advanced economies remove accounts payable and receivable, as well as equity holdings, but Canada includes equity assets, and both accounts payable and receivable.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-IMF2026-48):49–50 The IMF's general government gross debt calculation excludes unfunded pension liabilities, to maintain comparability with other countries.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-IMF2026-48):50

[edit]
A 2024 report by the Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO) said that the current fiscal policy of the federal government, and the provinces of Quebec, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, Ontario, and Alberta, were sustainable over the long-term. A country’s national debt, also known as government debt or public debt, is defined as all borrowings owed by the government of a country. It usually comprises internal debt – owed to other governmental departments – and external debt, which is held by the public and is owed to government bond owners. National debt can be caused by a struggling economy in general, or by low tax income, which usually leads to money being borrowed from other governments for support, which in turn cannot be paid back right away. At first glance, a high national debt is not always a sign of a struggling economy – but since increasing debt can slow down economic growth significantly, it is imperative for the respective government to seek a steady reduction in the long run.

## Debt held by foreign investors
[edit]
In 1960, 4% of the Canadian government debt was held by foreign investors.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-40) Non-resident investors held 35% of Government of Canada securities in 2024/25. The Department of Finance described this as "in line with the average share for G7 countries." The share of foreign-resident holdings has been relatively stable since 2015-16.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-41)

## Risk factors: interest rates and economic growth
[edit]
Major risk factors that can increase government debt include slowing economic growth and rising interest rates.
Rising interest rates increase public debt charges, raising government expenditures.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Kerim-Dikeni_L%C3%A9onard_20210914-1) From 2011 to 2021, falling interest rates meant that, while public debt rose, public debt charges decreased from $29 billion to $24 billion.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Kerim-Dikeni_L%C3%A9onard_20210914-1) The average interest rate paid on the federal debt was 4.6% in the fiscal year 2007/08,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Kerim-Dikeni_L%C3%A9onard_20210914-1) and in 2020/21 it was 1.4%.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-DFC_2022-42):49 Rates at that time were by far the lowest in the post-war period.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Drummond_20201020-43) By 2024/25, consolidated general government interest expenses reached $102.4 billion ($50.1 billion for the federal government, and $52.5 billion for the provincial, territorial and local governments), due to higher debt refinancing interest rates and higher government gross debt.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Daily20251121-4) Measured as a share of total government revenue, the consolidated general government interest expense in 2024/25 was 9%.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Daily20251121-4)

## Risk factors: interest rates and economic growth
Slow economic growth is a risk factor since it means government tax revenue grows less quickly. Further, slower growth of GDP relative to growth of debt increases the ratio of debt to GDP.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Drummond_20201020-43)

## Debt comparison with other countries
[edit]
The level of government responsible for government programs differs across countries. For this reason, international fiscal comparisons are usually made on a total government, national accounts basis. For Canada, total government includes the federal (central), provincial/territorial, and local governments. Another reason to measure debt on a total government basis is that the federal government may be viewed as responsible for the debt of other levels of government.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-44)Credit rating agency Fitch said it expects the federal government to provide a province with access to debt markets, as it did early in the coronavirus pandemic.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-46) When Newfoundland needed debt repayment assistance in March 2020, it appealed to the federal government.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-47) Any aid delivered to one province would reduce the resources the federal government has available for its own debt repayment responsibilities, and to support debt repayment in other provinces.

## Debt comparison with other countries
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) reports that in 2024 Canada's net and gross debt-to-GDP ratios were 11% and 110%, respectively.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-IMF2026-48) Canada's general government holds sizeable financial assets (approximately 99% measured as a percentage of GDP at market value at end-2024), with around 30% invested in equity shares, of which more than half relate to pension fund investments.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-IMF2026-48):49–50 Financial assets rose sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic (to 81% of GDP in 2021 from 64% in 2019), spurred by support measures such as loans to businesses and tax deferrals (accounts receivable).[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-IMF2022-49):39 Canada's general government gross debt includes substantial accounts payable (around 18% of GDP at end-2024), which many advanced countries do not report.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-IMF2026-48):49–50 In net debt calculations, most advanced economies remove accounts payable and receivable, as well as equity holdings, but Canada includes equity assets, and both accounts payable and receivable.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-IMF2026-48):49–50 The IMF's general government gross debt calculation excludes unfunded pension liabilities, to maintain comparability with other countries.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-IMF2026-48):50

## Debt comparison with other countries
The general government gross debt-to-GDP ratio for countries the IMF classifies as Advanced economies that have a population of at least 5 million is shown in the table below. In 2025, Canada had the third lowest level of gross public debt as a percent of GDP among the G7 countries – lower than Japan, Italy, the United States, and France, but higher than Germany, and the United Kingdom.

## Public debt sustainability
[edit]
A 2024 report by the Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO) said that the current fiscal policy of the federal government, and the provinces of Quebec, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, Ontario, and Alberta, were sustainable over the long-term. This was not the case for the remaining provincial and territorial governments.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-PBO2024-9) A province with an unsustainable fiscal trajectory must eventually introduce permanent tax increases and/or spending reductions in order to keep its net debt-to-GDP ratio below its initial level over a 75-year projection horizon.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-PBOreport2024-51)
The PBO identified the main driver of government debt as a demographic shift, as the older population transitions into retirement and the workforce growth slows. The aging population will also raise financial pressure on provincial programs such as healthcare and public pensions.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-PBO2024-9)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-PBOreport2024-51)
As of 2025, Canada maintained its AAA sovereign credit rating from S&P, [Moody's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody's_Ratings "Moody's Ratings"), and Morningstar DBRS.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-StArnaud-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-53)Fitch downgraded its credit rating for Canada from AAA to AA+ in June 2020, following a period of record deficits during the COVID-19 pandemic.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-54)

## Public debt sustainability
A credit rating provides an indication of the sustainability of a government's debt, as it shows the rating agency's view of the ability of a borrower to meet its financial commitments.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-Fitch-55) Credit rating agency reports on Canada's credit strength are used by investors—including sovereign wealth and pension funds.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-tradingeconomics_2022-56) A credit rating may affect borrowing costs.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_public_debt#cite_note-57)

# General government gross debt as a share of gross domestic product in the European Union in 2nd quarter 2026, by member state
A country’s national debt, also known as government debt or public debt, is defined as all borrowings owed by the government of a country. It usually comprises internal debt – owed to other governmental departments – and external debt, which is held by the public and is owed to government bond owners. National debt can be caused by a struggling economy in general, or by low tax income, which usually leads to money being borrowed from other governments for support, which in turn cannot be paid back right away. At first glance, a high national debt is not always a sign of a struggling economy – but since increasing debt can slow down economic growth significantly, it is imperative for the respective government to seek a steady reduction in the long run.
